title: CHRISTIANS VISITING PROSTITUTES? PAUL HAD TO CONFRONT THIS INSIDE THE CHURCH
paragraphs: CHRISTIANS VISITING PROSTITUTES? PAUL HAD TO CONFRONT THIS INSIDE THE CHURCH
The shocking words of 1 Corinthians 6 reveal something far deeper than a sexual scandal: what happens when someone who belongs to Jesus tries to give Christ’s body to a secret sin.
There is a sentence in the New Testament so uncomfortable that we can read straight past it without feeling its weight.
Paul was writing to Christians.
People who knew the name of Jesus.
People gathering as the church.
People Paul had just reminded that they had been washed, sanctified, and justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ.
And then Paul asked them a question that should make every Christian stop.
“Shall I then take the members of Christ and make them members of a prostitute?”
Think about what had to be happening for an apostle to write that sentence.
Not to pagan Rome.
Not as a lecture about how disgusting outsiders were.
To the church.
Paul’s words in 1 Corinthians 6:15 are even more jarring in the Greek:
“ἄρας οὖν τὰ μέλη τοῦ Χριστοῦ ποιήσω πόρνης μέλη; μὴ γένοιτο.”
Literally, the thought is: Shall I take away the members of Christ and make them members of a prostitute?
Then comes Paul’s horrified answer:
“μὴ γένοιτο.”
Mē genoito.
Absolutely not.
May it never be.
Paul was confronting something many Christians still struggle to understand two thousand years later.
You can belong to Christ and still be tempted to carry your body somewhere your confession says it should never go.
You can sing worship songs while hiding browser history.
You can quote Scripture while maintaining a secret conversation you would panic to see projected on the church wall.
You can lift your hands on Sunday while using those same hands during the week in ways that leave you ashamed.
You can know Christian vocabulary and still be losing a private war.
That does not make sin harmless.
It makes grace desperately necessary.
And perhaps somebody reading this has already become uncomfortable.
Good.
Not because humiliation is the goal.
Jesus is.
Because sometimes conviction is mercy knocking on a locked door.
Paul was not merely telling the Corinthians, “Sex outside God’s design is against the rules.”
His argument went much deeper.
He was telling them:
You have forgotten who your body belongs to.
Earlier in the passage, Paul writes:
“The body is not for sexual immorality, but for the Lord.”
That word translated “sexual immorality” is πορνεία — porneia.
It refers broadly to sexual immorality, not merely prostitution. A few verses later Paul uses πόρνη — pornē, specifically referring to a prostitute.
And notice the argument.
Paul does not say your body is worthless because you sinned.
He says almost exactly the opposite.
Your body matters so much that it belongs to the Lord.
Christianity is not a religion in which the “spiritual” part of you belongs to Jesus while your physical life remains private property.
Your eyes belong to Him.
Your hands belong to Him.
Your sexuality belongs to Him.
Your phone at 1:17 in the morning belongs under His lordship.
Your hotel room belongs under His lordship.
Your private messages belong under His lordship.
Your desires belong under His lordship.
Even the parts of your life nobody else sees are lived before the One who bought you.
Then Paul says something staggering.
“οὐκ οἴδατε ὅτι τὰ σώματα ὑμῶν μέλη Χριστοῦ ἐστιν;”
“Do you not know that your bodies are members of Christ?”
That changes everything.
Paul’s argument is not simply, “A Christian should behave better.”
It is:
You are joined to Christ.
Your body is not spiritually irrelevant.
What you do with your body cannot be separated neatly from whom your body belongs to.
That is why Paul immediately asks whether he should take the members of Christ and make them members of a prostitute.
“μὴ γένοιτο.”
Never.
And then Paul reaches all the way back to Genesis:
“The two shall become one flesh.”
Sex, biblically understood, was never designed to be the meaningless collision of two bodies.
Paul says:
“ὁ κολλώμενος τῇ πόρνῃ ἓν σῶμά ἐστιν.”
“The one who joins himself to a prostitute is one body with her.”
The word κολλώμενος — kollōmenos carries the idea of joining, attaching, clinging.
Paul refuses the fantasy that a person can say, “It was only physical.”
The body is involved.
The person is involved.
Something God designed with profound meaning is involved.
And then comes one of the most beautiful contrasts in the passage:
“ὁ δὲ κολλώμενος τῷ κυρίῳ ἓν πνεῦμά ἐστιν.”
“But the one who is joined to the Lord is one spirit with Him.”
Joined to the prostitute.
Joined to the Lord.
Paul places the two realities almost painfully close together.
And suddenly this ancient Corinthian confrontation becomes a mirror.
Because maybe you have never paid a prostitute.
But perhaps you know what it is to be divided.
You love Jesus...
but there is something you keep returning to.
Pornography.
An affair.
Sexual conversations nobody knows about.
A relationship you keep trying to rename because calling it what Scripture calls it would require a decision.
A secret account.
A fantasy.
A habit you promised God you would quit after the last time.
Then the last time became another time.
Then another.
Until eventually you stopped promising.
Maybe your secret is not sexual at all.
Maybe it is alcohol.
Bitterness.
Greed.
Gambling.
Dishonesty.
Pride.
An addiction nobody suspects.
A hatred you have carefully dressed in religious language.
Paul’s immediate subject here is sexual immorality, and we should not dilute that. But the deeper question still reaches every hidden room:
Who owns you?
Because Paul eventually gives the Corinthians one of the shortest commands in the passage:
“φεύγετε τὴν πορνείαν.”
Flee sexual immorality.
Not negotiate with it.
Not see how close you can stand to it.
Not keep its phone number “just in case.”
Not ask how much you can get away with and still call yourself Christian.
Flee.
There are temptations Scripture tells us to resist.
Here, Scripture says run.
Sometimes the most spiritual thing you can do is leave the room.
Delete the number.
Block the account.
End the conversation.
Cancel the meeting.
Tell somebody trustworthy what has been happening.
Stop carrying a smartphone into the place where you repeatedly fall.
Confess.
Bring the darkness into the light.
Run toward Christ while running away from the thing destroying you.
But this is where some Christians hear Paul incorrectly.
They hear:
“Flee because God is disgusted with you.”
That is not Paul’s argument.
Keep reading.
“Do you not know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit within you, whom you have from God?”
A temple.
Read that again.
Paul is speaking to believers he is correcting severely, and he reminds them of the Holy Spirit’s presence.
Then he writes:
“You are not your own.”
Those words offend the modern instinct.
My body.
My choice.
My desires.
My rules.
My truth.
Paul overturns the entire vocabulary of self-ownership with one sentence.
You are not your own.
Why?
Here comes the Gospel.
“ἠγοράσθητε γὰρ τιμῆς.”
“For you were bought with a price.”
There it is.
The scandal underneath the scandal.
The Christian caught in sexual sin was not being called back merely to morality.
He was being called back to the Cross.
A price had been paid.
Jesus Christ did not purchase His people with silver.
Not with gold.
Not with religious performance.
He gave Himself.
The sinless Son of God entered our ruin.
He bore sin.
He died.
He rose.
And the Christian life begins to make sense only when we understand that grace does not mean, “My sin no longer matters.”
Grace means my sin mattered so terribly that Christ went to the Cross—and He loved sinners so deeply that He went willingly.
This is where shame wants to interrupt.
Shame says:
“You have gone too far.”
Jesus says to repent and come.
Shame says:
“If people knew what you had done, everything would be over.”
The Gospel says your salvation was never built upon pretending you had never sinned.
Shame says:
“Hide.”
Christ calls sinners into the light.
And Scripture had already prepared the Corinthians for this moment.
Only a few verses earlier, after naming serious patterns of sin, Paul says something breathtaking:
“καὶ ταῦτά τινες ἦτε.”
“And such were some of you.”
Were.
Not because their histories disappeared.
Not because the consequences magically vanished.
Not because yesterday had never happened.
But because Jesus had entered the story.
Paul continues by reminding them that they had been washed, sanctified, and justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of God.
That is Christianity.
Not clean people congratulating themselves for never becoming dirty.
Sinners washed by Christ.
Not people with spotless histories.
People with a Savior.
Not people saying, “Look what I overcame.”
People saying, “Look what Jesus did.”
Perhaps that is why this passage hurts so beautifully.
Paul refuses to lower God’s standard.
Sexual immorality is still sin.
Prostitution does not suddenly become holy because a Christian participates in it.
Pornography does not become harmless because everybody has a phone.
Adultery does not become acceptable because a marriage became difficult.
Secret sin does not become less destructive because nobody discovered it.
Grace never requires us to rename darkness.
But neither does Paul tell the repentant sinner that darkness gets the final word.
Jesus does.
That is the heartbeat of the Gospel.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by calling the scandal righteousness.
Not by pretending sin never happened.

He rewrites everything by forgiving sinners, cleansing the guilty, breaking chains, restoring what sin devastated, giving His Spirit, and creating a new life where shame once thought it owned the ending.
Maybe your scandal is known by thousands.
Maybe it is known by five people.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe your spouse does not know.
Your pastor does not know.
Your parents do not know.
Your children do not know.
Your friends would never imagine it.
But God knows.
And astonishingly...
He is still calling you.
Not deeper into hiding.
Home.
There is a difference between conviction and condemnation.
Conviction says, “This must come into the light.”
Condemnation says, “You should stay in the darkness because someone like you could never be loved.”
One leads toward repentance.
The other tries to keep you chained to shame.
Listen again to Paul.
After everything he says about sexual sin, prostitution, one flesh, fleeing immorality, and belonging to God, his final command is not:
“Despise your body.”
It is:
“δοξάσατε δὴ τὸν θεὸν ἐν τῷ σώματι ὑμῶν.”
“Therefore glorify God in your body.”
Glorify.
God.
In your body.
The same body temptation tried to claim.
The same body sin tried to use.
The same body shame told you was permanently contaminated.
Give it to Christ.
Your body can become an instrument of obedience.
Your eyes can learn purity.
Your hands can serve.
Your mouth can speak truth.
Your sexuality can come under the lordship of Jesus.
Your private life can become consistent with your public worship.
Your scars can become reminders that Christ did not abandon you in the battle.
Your testimony can someday help another trembling Christian whisper:
“Maybe Jesus can rescue me too.”
And if you are currently trapped, do not mistake reading an emotional article for repentance.
Do something.
Confess your sin to God.
Turn from it.
Where another person has been harmed, seek wise, truthful, responsible counsel about making things right without creating further harm.
Bring trustworthy Christian accountability into the secret.
Remove access to what repeatedly pulls you back.
And stop trying to defeat in secrecy what secrecy has been feeding.
Jesus did not die merely to make you feel guilty for five minutes.
He died and rose to reconcile sinners to God and bring them into new life.
And perhaps somebody you know desperately needs to hear this.
Not so you can publicly expose them.
Never use Scripture as a weapon for humiliation.
And if Christ has already brought you through a hidden season of bondage, consider commenting:
Somebody reading beneath you may need your testimony more than you realize.
But there is something else worth saying carefully.
We glorify God by belonging to Christ and living faithfully before Him.
But generosity, sharing biblical truth, encouraging other believers, and helping sound Gospel ministry reach people can certainly become practical expressions of that devotion.

So if this ministry is feeding you spiritually and you want to help Gospel Warrior keep placing Christ-centered truth in front of people who may never walk voluntarily into a church building, we invite you to stand with us.
Not because an algorithm deserves your attention.
Because perhaps someone behind a smiling profile picture is secretly wondering whether Jesus still wants them after what they did last night.
Let them find the answer.
Sin is serious.
Repentance is necessary.
The Cross was costly.
Grace is real.
Jesus still saves.
And your worst chapter does not have the authority to write the final sentence when the pen belongs to Christ.
The secret you thought would become your ending may become the very place where you finally discover how desperately you need the Savior.
